newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Top UN food aid official due in N.Korea at weekend.
newsitem.headline: Top UN food aid official due in N.Korea at weekend.

text.p: The American head of the World Food Programme arrives in North Korea on Saturday to visit areas damaged by flooding, where malnourished people could begin dying by this summer unless aid arrives, a spokeswoman said on Friday.

Catherine Bertini, a former U.S. assistant secretary of agriculture who heads the Rome-based U.N. agency, is to meet top officials in the isolated Stalinist state during a three-day trip. They include vice president Li Jong-Ok and deputy prime minister and chairman of public welfare Kong Jin-tae.
"Mrs. Bertini is the highest level U.N. official to go to the country since the start of the crisis two years ago," WFP spokeswoman Christiane Berthiaume told a news briefing.
"She will visit areas affected by flooding whose population is already in danger," she added. "She will meet the country's authorities to see how one can respond better to this crisis."
Berthiaume later told Reuters: "People are getting thinner and thinner because they are giving their food to the children. If nothing happens, people could start dying by this summer."
Floods in 1995 and 1996 drowned rice fields, washed away roads and left half a million North Koreans homeless out of a population of 23 million, according to relief organisations.
Aid agencies have warned of potential famine in North Korea, although they say foreign aid, rationing and the efficient food distribution system have averted starvation so far.
Some 400,000 hectares of farm land were destroyed by the floods as well as two million tonnes of seeds, according to WFP.
North Korea, which has a food deficit of 2.36 million tonnes, is only able to import about 500,000 tonnes, according to WFP figures. This leaves a shortfall of 1.8 million tonnes.
But WFP can only raise the equivalent of 100,000 tonnes, meaning the roughly 1.7 million tonne shortfall has to be filled through bilateral contributions to the reclusive state.
Civilians are receiving only between 100 and 200 grams of food daily from the government's distribution system.
"That is about one-half a bowl of rice, which represents about one-sixth of the ration distributed daily to refugees and other people in crisis situations elsewhere," Berthiaume said.

"It is estimated that the North Koreans, through various means, actually get the equivalent of 320 grams of food a day, but this is 20 per cent less than a person should normally receive to stay healthy," she added.

A month ago, WFP appealed for $41 million to stave off "a real possibility of famine" in North Korea. The funds would buy 100,000 tonnes of food aid over the next year for 1.7 million of the most vulnerable flood victims, mainly farmers and children.
So far, donor countries have contributed half of the amount sought in cash and in kind, according to Berthiaume.
Bertini is also to meet North Korea's deputy minister for foreign affairs Choe Sun Hon and vice minister of the agriculture committee Kim Yong Suk.

The 46-year-old New Yorker was reppointed last month by the United Nations to a second five year term as WFP executive director. The agency, the largest international food aid organisation in the world, employs 4,000 humanitarian workers in emergency and development operations in more than 90 countries.
